Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a single, continuous scene in real-time—a short ferry crossing featuring grounded physical actions and concise dialogue between Ilse and her son, Jonas. Woven seamlessly into the pauses of this scene are brief moments of exposition and summary. Through Ilse's internal reflections, the reader learns necessary background information—such as how Jonas behaved as a child, the death of Henning four years prior, and the gradual decline of passengers using the ferry over the years—without ever halting the momentum of the present-time crossing. This balance keeps the story engaging while lending emotional weight and history to the characters' sparse interactions.
